top_choice_rationale: P001 (Autor, Hanson, Katz) best meets the common criteria. It pairs a mature framework for how technology and trade shift labour demand and wage structure with design-based local-labour-market evidence. The skill-premium line is about three decades old, the task framework over two decades and the China-shock papers over a decade. The work has been replicated, extended and heavily criticised, and the open disputes concern magnitude and persistence, not whether the effects exist. A citation on labour demand, wage structure and local adjustment can be drafted without claiming origination of the task framework or restating the 2023 and 2024 prizes. The attribution problem is smaller than in the alternatives I considered, such as the eight-name B004 set. Katz's separate wage-structure and skill-premium credit is the weakest link, and Dorn's exclusion under the three-name cap is a real cost. I therefore rank P002 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) second as the principled fallback if the committee cannot draft one citation covering both strands. P002 is still clearly preferable to making no award, so P000 is last.
